BaFin publishes supervisory notice on subdued credit demand; moreover, refinancing costs increased.
II
Outsourcing to cloud providers Savings banks and cooperative
On February 1, 2024, BaFin published a supervisory notice for outsourcing to cloud providers. It is based on the BaFin guidance from November 2018. The supervisory notice provides practical insights into how BaFin assesses outsourcing to cloud providers. In addition, the supervisory notice offers guidance for supervised companies and already takes into account the requirements of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

1.2 Development of the institutions

1.2.1 German institutions under direct supervision of the ECB

In total, 25 German banking groups were classified as significant institutions in 2024. They were thus under the direct supervision of the European Central Bank (ECB) within the framework of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). BaFin participated in the joint supervisory teams of the SSM.

1.2.2 Institutions under direct supervision of BaFin

Private, regional, and specialized banks
The earnings situation of private, regional, and specialized banks was predominantly positive in 2024 – apart from the formation of risk provisions. However, the economic situation caused the rates of non-performing loans (NPL ratios) to rise. In particular, institutions engaged in commercial real estate financing had to expand their risk provisioning. The still attractive interest rate of the ECB for deposit facilities enabled the institutions to offer attractive interest rates and to refinance more diversely.

BaFin closely accompanied some institutions in remedying deficiencies that it had observed more closely due to their improper business organization. In some cases, BaFin lifted capital surcharges in 2024 after the institutions had addressed the deficiencies. The supervisory authority strives to further develop and harmonize supervisory requirements. In 2024, it published a consultation on the further development of the collective management report of building societies.

Savings banks and cooperative banks
The cooperative banks and savings banks continued to benefit from the interest rate environment. In addition, the number of loan defaults among corporate customers as well as private customers increased only moderately despite the stagnant economy. In their securities investments, the institutions recorded slight value recoveries. This was offset by a subdued credit demand; moreover, refinancing costs increased. Savings banks and cooperative banks still achieved satisfactory annual results, which enabled them to strengthen their equity base. Nevertheless, there were individual, exceptionally costly restructuring cases among cooperative banks. The reason for this was errors in risk management and in the governance of the banks.

A challenge was the increasing shortage of skilled workers, especially in IT and generally at small institutions. Therefore, savings banks and cooperative banks have increasingly invested in their staff. Mergers and outsourcing are also options to meet this challenge and the strong competition in the German financial sector. The trend towards mergers continued in both sectors (see Chart 3 and 4, page 42). The number of savings banks and cooperative banks is therefore continuing to decline.11

Due to the high importance of outsourcing in the cooperative bank and savings bank sector, this was also a focus of supervision in 2024. Both sectors continuously expanded the services of their outsourcing companies and developed them further, also in view of changed and increased supervisory requirements. If the supervisory authority identified a need for adjustments at institutions in 2024, it accompanied them closely.

Building societies
In 2024, the consolidation of the building society sector continued. Due to its balance sheet growth, Wüstenrot Bausparkasse AG was for the first time under the direct supervision of the ECB on an individual institution basis in 2024. BaFin intensively accompanied this process as part of the responsible Joint-Supervisory Teams of the ECB. Supervision according to the Building Societies Act remains with BaFin.

In 2024, new building society business declined. The building societies predominantly responded to the changed interest rate environment with adjustments to the building savings tariff conditions.

The supervisory authority is committed to further developing and standardizing supervisory requirements. In 2024, it published a consultation on the further development of the collective management report of building societies.

"2 Highlights of Supervisory Practice
I
2.1 More Proportionality – Less Establishment. It critically questions its administrative practices
Complexity and Bureaucracy and adjusts them when necessary. A milestone
in banking supervision is the supervisory communication,
The BaFin advocates for less complexity and more proportionality in regulation and supervision. It is
important to them not to lower the level of security. Especially in the calibration of solvency requirements
of Basel III and Solvency II, no compromises should be made. From BaFin's point of view, instead,
complexity and bureaucratic effort must be contained. The goal is effective and, in case of doubt, strict, but easily understandable rules.

Less complex and simpler rules are particularly important for smaller institutions and companies. Especially
for them, overly complex regulations and supervisory requirements pose a burden. The regulation
for these institutions and companies must be designed to be more proportional and risk-appropriate.

De-bureaucratization as a Permanent Theme
Of the total 69 annual goals of BaFin for 2024, 14 were about reducing bureaucratic effort or accelerating processes. BaFin has
furthermore established de-bureaucratization as a continuous process at the end of 2024. It intends to regularly compile proposals for
de-bureaucratization of national and European law and submit them to the Federal Ministry of Finance for future legislative initiatives.
Twelve of BaFin's proposals from 2024 have been incorporated into the government draft of the Future Financing Act II. These included the abolition of the employee and complaint register and the elimination
of land registry certificates for open and closed real estate special funds.

Less Complexity at the EU Level
In addition, BaFin is also advocating for less complexity in European regulation, especially at the European supervisory authorities and in Level-2/Level-3 activities. It has also submitted 27 proposals for de-bureaucratization of European law to the Federal Ministry of Finance. They mainly concern the elimination of notification, reporting, and approval obligations, the adjustment
of threshold values, and the abolition of overregulation and more proportionality.

BaFin Questions Its Own Administrative Practice
Even in areas that BaFin can shape itself,
it wants less complex, proportional rules.

2.2 Risk Classification and (Special) Audits

2.2.1 Credit Institutions, Payment and
E-Money Institutions, Leasing and
Factoring Institutions, Crypto Custodians,
Crypto Securities Register Management
and Credit Service Institutions
under the Credit Secondary Market Act

Risk Classification
BaFin and the Deutsche Bundesbank create an annual risk analysis for the credit institutions under their national supervision. The basis for this: A guideline from the European Banking Authority (EBA) on the supervisory review and evaluation process (SREP). In line with this guideline, the European Central Bank (ECB) publishes the SSM-LSI-SREP methodology to ensure a uniform approach for less significant institutions (Less Significant Institutions – LSIs) within the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). The ECB continuously develops and
adapts this methodology to changes in the banking sector.

BaFin classifies credit institutions based on two dimensions: the quality of the institution, which can range from 1 (very good) to 4 (poor) according to the SREP result, and based on the potential impact of a solvency or liquidity crisis of the institution on the stability of the financial sector. This dimension ranges from I
(low) to IV (high, see Table 1, page 17). From this classification, BaFin derives the intensity of its supervisory program for the individual institution. In this way, it ensures a proportional, risk-oriented supervisory approach.

translation.en_XX:
Preface
2024 was marked by geopolitical tensions, political uncertainty, and a faltering economic performance in Germany. How did we at BaFin deal with this situation and the risks that arose from it? What issues did we focus on in 2024? And what priorities did we set? You will find answers to these questions in this annual report.

The following pages make it clear: Our nearly 3,000 employees have committed themselves in various ways over the past year to a functional, honest, and stable financial system that companies and individuals can trust.

Throughout the past year, we have worked intensively to make our supervisory requirements for credit institutions more proportional, in order to relieve small institutions of bureaucratic burdens. In November, we published a supervisory notice in which we demonstrated the leeway small credit institutions have in their risk management. In addition, this supervisory notice introduced facilitations. About three-quarters of German credit institutions are likely to benefit from this.

Furthermore, in 2024 we committed ourselves to reducing complexity in regulation and submitted corresponding proposals to the political decision-makers. We will also make concrete proposals to the new federal government on how we can reduce complexity in Germany and Europe and achieve more proportionality in financial market supervision and regulation.

There have been several changes within BaFin itself over the past year. On January 1, 2024, mathematician and actuary Julia Wiens took over as Executive Director of the Insurance and Pension Fund Supervision. In December 2024, we announced that Raimund Röseler, Executive Director of Banking Supervision, will retire at the end of March 2025. His successor, Nikolas Speer, took over on April 1, 2025.

The current year 2025 also presents some uncertainties for the financial industry. The geopolitical situation seems unstable, and the economy continues to develop sluggishly. At the same time, the digital transformation of the financial industry is rapidly advancing. We will continue to work to ensure that bank customers, insured persons, as well as investors can trust the German financial system.

Mark Branson
President of BaFin, May 2025

BaFin updates the interpretative and application notes for the Anti-Money Laundering Act
On November 29, 2024, BaFin published the updated General Part of the Interpretative and Application Notes (AuA AT) on the Anti-Money Laundering Act. The notes are addressed to all entities supervised by BaFin under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (GwG). The publication was preceded by an extensive public consultation process. The updated version contains, in addition to specifications of supervisory expectations, significant innovations. These include, among other things, the shortening of the maximum periods for the periodic updating of customer information and the guidance on risk classification of customers following a suspicious activity report.

The obligation to obtain a permit must be recognized as early as possible and sustainably prevented. The legislator has equipped them with effective investigative powers for this purpose. Against formal measures and measures of administrative enforcement, the addressees may file an objection.7 In total, 24 objection notices were issued in 2024 (previous year: 23).

BaFin can investigate potential operators of unauthorized businesses and possibly involved companies. This not only concerns the suspicious company but also current and former executives and employees. BaFin can inspect suspicious companies on-site or have them inspected by the Deutsche Bundesbank. Specifically, it can search business premises, ancillary rooms, and persons. In principle, this is done on the basis of a judicial order, but exceptionally also on the basis of its own order in case of imminent danger. BaFin is also allowed to search residential premises. However, a judicial order is required in every case.

BaFin makes its measures and warnings known on its website. This serves consumer protection. Illegally operated crypto ATMs attract users with criminal intentions and pose a money laundering risk.

The focus on the pursuit of unauthorized businesses in 2024 was also on combating unlicensed, fraudulent online trading platforms, as well as fraudulent pre-IPO stock offers and illegal fixed-term deposit offers. Often, these were associated with identity misuse or identity theft.

The number of suspected cases was again high in 2024, as Table 15 shows. The formal measures even reached a new record high.

2.3.7.3 Action Day: Seizure of Crypto ATMs

In a nationwide action at a total of 35 locations, BaFin secured 13 crypto ATMs in August 2024, where Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies could be traded and which were operated without the required BaFin permission. BaFin was supported by the police and the Deutsche Bundesbank and coordinated with the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) against the operators of the machines.

Exchanging euros for cryptocurrencies and vice versa constitutes commercial proprietary trading or a banking business. For this, operators require BaFin's permission according to § 32 KWG. Illegally operated crypto ATMs attract users with criminal intentions and pose a money laundering risk.

2.3.8 (Fraudulent) Public Offers

In 2024, BaFin published 26 warnings due to the suspicion of prospectus-free offers (previous year 36). Furthermore, the number of information and document requests increased from 14 to 26. BaFin referred eleven cases from market supervision to law enforcement authorities (previous year 26). In one case, BaFin definitively prohibited a public offering of securities.

Practical examples

In 2024, BaFin also proceeded against public offers of securities and investments with a presumably criminal background. In many such cases, it can effectively support the criminal investigation authorities. For example, in one case, it provided indications of fraudulent behavior to the competent public prosecutor's office. The tip led to an extensive investigation for suspicion of fraud involving hundreds of millions. The proceedings were not yet concluded at the time of editing.

In 2024, BaFin conducted 134 special audits (previous year: 153). Table 3 shows how the special audits were distributed across the different groups of institutions as well as the focal points of the audits. BaFin also used other supervisory tools to gain insights into the supervised institutions: for example, setting priorities according to § 30 KWG in the annual audit.

2.2.2 Insurance Companies and Pension Funds

Risk Classification

BaFin also classifies supervised insurers and pension funds into risk categories to be able to supervise them in a risk-oriented and proportional manner (see Table 4, page 19).

In the classification, BaFin first considers the quality of a company or group. This is derived, among other things, from the asset, financial, and earnings situation, the business organization and future viability, as well as the holders of significant stakes.

For the assessment of groups, BaFin takes into account certain group-specific characteristics instead of the holders of significant stakes. BaFin considers both the classification results of the individual companies and qualitative and quantitative group-specific information. In 2024, the classified insurance groups received quality grades "A" (1.9 percent), "B" (81.1 percent), or "C" (17.0 percent).

Audits

BaFin also takes a risk-oriented approach in the planning of audits in insurance supervision. In addition to the results of the risk classification, it also considers, among other things, when the last audit took place at a supervised company. Furthermore, BaFin conducts event- and topic-related special audits, for example, with regard to IT or in the conduct of business supervision.

2.5.4 Machine Learning in Internal Models

Under the co-leadership of BaFin, a working group of the European Central Bank (ECB) formulated supervisory expectations for the use of machine learning in internal models of credit institutions. They were presented at an industry roundtable in October 2024 and discussed in several workshops with institutions. The supervisory expectations will be incorporated into the revision of the ECB Guide to Internal Models in spring 2025. The ECB working group consisted of ECB staff and representatives of national supervisory authorities.

2.6 Sustainable Finance

2.6.1 EU Disclosure Regulation
BaFin Sample on Disclosure Regulation
In 2024, BaFin conducted a non-representative sample survey on the implementation of the EU Disclosure Regulation (Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation – SFDR). The result: Financial market participants often use generally formulated pre-contractual information. This makes it difficult for investors to understand the ecological or social characteristics or objectives of the financial product. In addition, providers often use ESG ratings, which did not always seem suitable for an adequate statement on the sustainability characteristics of a financial product. BaFin demands that fund providers and other financial service providers do not adopt ESG ratings uncritically.

BaFin calls for easily understandable product categories
In 2024, BaFin called for the creation of easily understandable product categories with clear criteria that are consistent with existing sustainability definitions such as the EU taxonomy. Only financial products with a high minimum share of sustainable or transformative investments should be allowed to be advertised as sustainable. This is stipulated, for example, in the ESMA guidelines on fund names.

Q&As on SFDR developed
BaFin developed three "Questions & Answers" (Q&As) in 2024 to support German financial market participants in complying with SFDR requirements. These address the term "consider" in the context of the principal adverse impacts (Principal Adverse Impact – "PAI"), how derivatives must be treated within the disclosure regulation, and regular reports that institutions must publish. Furthermore, BaFin recommends highlighting controversially discussed investments such as arms investments prominently in a product advertised as sustainable.

2.6.2 Management of Climate and Environmental Risks
In 2024, BaFin conducted a non-representative survey among banks and insurance companies on physical climate risks. The survey revealed that the companies surveyed are generally dealing with ESG risks. However, banks in particular are sometimes still at an early stage. It also showed that data availability continues to be challenging for many companies.

2.6.3 Preparation for Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
In anticipation of the yet-to-be-implemented Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), BaFin is expected to be responsible for reviewing the sustainability reports of capital market-oriented issuers. It is keeping an eye on the current regulatory developments at the national and European levels for this purpose. To prepare, BaFin set up a specialized division in 2024. As soon as the legal prerequisites are in place, BaFin will commence its supervisory activities.

2.7 BaFin International

2.7.1 Bilateral and Multilateral Cooperation
Based on Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), BaFin works closely with foreign supervisory authorities. In the EU, cooperation takes place within the framework of the European System of Financial Supervision.

Examination Focus and Compliance with Anti-Terrorism Financing

I
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) designates uniform European priorities for audits of the previous business year on an annual basis. For the audits concerning the business year 2023, it identified climate-related issues and the macroeconomic environment, with a focus on refinancing risks arising from the general interest rate development (see Table 8).

In addition, BaFin set its own focus on the presentation of the business model and control system in the (group) management report. This was complemented by risk-oriented, selected company-specific focal points.

On November 7, 2024, BaFin published its examination focus for the random sample audits in 2025. The focus is on the recoverable value of financial and non-financial assets.

First Forum on Financial Reporting Control
On November 7, 2024, BaFin hosted the Forum on Financial Reporting Control and Corporate Reporting in Frankfurt am Main for the first time. It provided information on its supervisory priorities and current findings from previous audits. In addition, BaFin auditors exchanged views with representatives of supervised companies, auditors, and other stakeholders. Topics of discussion included the challenges of future sustainability reporting.

Findings from the 2023 anti-terrorism financing audit campaign were taken into account by BaFin in its supervisory activities in 2024. To verify its results, it re-audited institutions in 2024 that had previously been part of the campaign. It became clear in these and routine audits that institutions need to more clearly differentiate their measures against money laundering and terrorism financing and deal more intensively with institution-specific risks. BaFin has published information on this on its website.

In addition to the audits, BaFin conducted 672 regular or event-driven supervisory discussions or visits in 2024 (previous year: 628).

2.2.5 Anti-Money Laundering Prevention
In 35 annual audits for the year 2024, BaFin set additional examination priorities to intensively audit institution-specific prevention measures.

Legal Review by BaFin 2.4.2 Product Intervention

From this point on, BaFin is no longer responsible for handling the objection procedure. Through product intervention, BaFin can restrict or prohibit the marketing, distribution, or sale of a financial instrument if there are significant concerns for investor protection. In 2024, BaFin initiated 39 proceedings to examine significant investor protection concerns (previous year: 37). 18 of these proceedings were conclusively dealt with during the reporting year. After BaFin confronted the providers with the investor protection concerns, three of the 18 providers ceased their offer during the ongoing product intervention proceedings. Another provider adjusted the product. In the other cases, further examinations showed that the conditions for a product intervention were not met.

Additionally, five providers submitted or adjusted their offers during the ongoing product intervention proceedings. BaFin had initiated proceedings against them in the years 2023 or 2022 and concluded them in 2024.

2.4 Consumer Protection

2.4.1 New Foundations of Supervisory Practice

BaFin Account Comparison
On March 15, 2024, the supervisory authority published the Regulation on Reporting of Payment Accounts for the Comparison Website (VglWebMV). It specifies the comparison criteria and data that payment service providers must report to BaFin so that consumers can compare current and basic accounts offered in Germany on the comparison website. The BaFin account comparison provides a broad and neutral overview of accounts and providers. The use is free of charge. The launch of the comparison website: January 15, 2025.

MaComp Circular Updated
In 2024, BaFin updated twice the minimum requirements for the compliance function and other conduct, organizational, and transparency obligations for securities services companies (MaComp).

In February 2024, it incorporated the European Securities and Markets Authority ESMA's guidelines on "certain aspects of the MiFID II remuneration requirements" (ESMA/35-43-3565) into the Special Part (BT) 8 of MaComp. In September 2024, it adopted the ESMA guidelines "on the product governance requirements of MiFID II" and "on certain aspects of the MiFID II suitability requirements" into BT 5 and BT 7.1 of MaComp.

2.4.3 Consumer-Protective Conduct and Market Supervision

General Administrative Act on Bonus Savings Adjusted
In October 2024, BaFin updated its general administrative act on bonus savings contracts. The background: In two judgments, the Federal Court of Justice (BGH) for the first time recognized a specific reference interest rate in July 2024 to recalculate interest on bonus savings contracts with ineffective interest rate adjustment clauses. At the same time, the court left open to what extent other interest rates can be used. Thus, a generally binding judicial supplementary contract interpretation is no longer to be expected, to which BaFin had referred in its general administrative act in June 2021. BaFin maintained the regulatory content of the order in the updated act and adjusted it textually so that further civil judicial supplementary contract interpretations are covered by the general administrative act.

translation.en_XX:
Since February 2024, the "Vision 2028" has been decisive for the work of the SRB within the SRM. It defines the new strategic objectives. In order to further improve the resolvability of institutions, the focus of resolution planning has shifted from plan creation to testing. For this purpose, the BaFin is intensively working on the creation of methodological foundations within the SRB.

Bank Levy
In preparation for bail-ins, BaFin conducted comprehensive test runs for ten German SRB banks in 2024. The focus was on data provision under real-time conditions and how bail-ins affect the balance sheet, regulatory ratios, and taxes. For ten more German SRB banks, there were data-based test runs. The improvement of the crisis management capabilities of the authorities was another focus of work in 2024. The SRB and BaFin conducted a joint crisis simulation for this purpose.

BaFin Strengthens Resolvability of German Institutions
In the 2024 planning cycle, BaFin was responsible for resolution planning for 1,212 institutions or institution groups based in Germany. Together with them, it worked on improving resolvability. The basis was the circular "Minimum Requirements for Resolvability in the Context of Resolution Planning."

In fully integrated residential building insurance policies, elemental risks are included. Here too, there is the possibility of opting out.

Several life insurers had already increased their profit participation in 2023 and 2024. This trend continued with the declaration of profit participation for the year 2025. Policyholders thus participate in the higher returns from new investments and reinvestments.

Recalculation of the transitional measures for Solvency II
In June 2024, pursuant to Section 352 (3) of the Insurance Supervision Act (VAG), BaFin ordered a recalculation of the transitional measure for technical provisions (provision transitional – RT). 

The RT was introduced in 2016 to facilitate the transition for life insurers to the Solvency II supervisory regime. It allows insurance companies to reduce the technical provisions during the transition period until 2032 by a deduction amount that decreases continuously.

In most cases, the associated deduction amount was determined when the technical provisions under Solvency II were significantly higher than under Solvency I due to low interest rates. With the rise in interest rates since 2022, this has generally reversed. Coverage ratios have risen significantly. Therefore, the RT was mostly no longer appropriate in amount and could even set wrong incentives.

The goal of the recalculation is to adequately reflect the current market environment. For the majority of life insurers, the RT drops to zero. However, the RT is not withdrawn but dynamically adjusted to the changed market.

2.2.2 Development of Private Health Insurers

The industry's risk-bearing capacity was robust in the reporting year 2024 as well. However, insurance benefits in Private Health Insurance (PHI) rose more sharply in 2023 and 2024 than before, partly due to inflation.

As a result of this development, the premium adjustments required by the usual adjustment mechanism were high. BaFin's annual industry evaluation showed that the premium adjustments in comprehensive health insurance for the year 2025 affected about 85 percent of insured individuals in at least one main tariff. The adjustments averaged 13.9 percent. However, some insured persons also saw their premiums decrease. To limit premium increases, health insurers used a total of approximately 2.33 billion euros from the provisions for premium refunds.

2.2.3 Development of Property and Casualty Insurers

The business year of the 199 property and casualty insurers supervised by BaFin in 2024 was characterized by an inflation rate above the long-term average. Although the inflation rate fell again in 2024 compared to the previous year, the claims inflation relevant to property and casualty insurers remained at a high level.

The high claims inflation was particularly evident in motor vehicle insurance (motor liability insurance, other motor vehicle insurance), residential building insurance, and in the annual report 2024 II Corporate Supervision | 45

2.2.1 Development of Life Insurers

BaFin had already assessed the situation of life insurers as robust – despite the low-interest environment of the past years. The rise in interest rates in 2022 further improved the economic indicators of the companies and their risk-bearing capacity under Solvency II. Even though the interest rate level has recently fallen slightly again, risk-bearing capacity remained stable in 2024.

In 2024, the reference interest rate for calculating the additional interest reserve was, as in the two previous years, at 1.57 percent. Due to portfolio changes, the additional interest reserve was reduced industry-wide again – by 4.1 billion euros. The released funds benefit the policyholders through higher profit participation. It will largely depend on the future development of capital market interest rates when the additional interest reserve is significantly dissolved.

Since 2023, the supervisory authority has grouped affiliated institutions in the impact dimension "low", after some of them had been classified as "medium low" in previous years. The reason for this adjustment: For these institutions, the risk-oriented supervisory approach should be applied even more consistently.

In addition, BaFin and the Deutsche Bundesbank developed a comparable framework for risk classification in 2023 for payment and e-money institutions as well as leasing and factoring institutions. The goal is to further expand the risk-oriented supervisory approach for these institutions. These companies are very heterogeneous and not directly comparable to credit institutions. Therefore, depending on the group of institutions, the supervisory authority takes into account other dimensions when classifying risk.

After a pilot phase in 2024, these frameworks will also be used for 2025.

Audits and Special Audits
According to § 44 of the Banking Act (KWG), BaFin has the right to information and to order special audits with a specific cause (cause-related audits) and without a specific cause (routine audits). In routine audits, the risk classification of the institutions is generally taken into account. translation.en_XX:
The causes of these structural challenges were manifold: Geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions burdened the export economy. Problematic were also the high energy costs compared to international standards, which burdened German companies. Particularly affected were energy-intensive industries such as the chemical and metal industries, as well as paper and glass production.

These developments had direct effects on companies: The number of corporate insolvencies increased, which in turn led to a rise in distressed loans. Consequently, banks and insurance companies increased their credit risk provisioning, albeit at a low level.

The BaFin closely monitored the credit risks of German financial institutions. In doing so, it focused on institutions that had a pronounced exposure to industries that could be particularly affected by an economic downturn.

1.4 Cyber Risks

In 2024, the threat in cyberspace was higher than ever before. This was the assessment of the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI). The increasing digitalization and networking of all systems offer cybercriminals ever new points of attack. The consequences of such attacks can be devastating: from financial losses to reputational damage to systemic crises.

Significant companies in the financial sector operate critical infrastructures and are therefore particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks.

The methods of attack are diverse and are constantly being further developed by new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence and Quantum Computing. In 2024, serious operational or security incidents affecting a payment service or a significant outsourcing had to be reported to the BaFin. In 2024, BaFin received 329 reports of such payment incidents. Thus, the number of reports increased significantly compared to previous years. To mitigate risks, the supervisory authority increasingly examined the IT of credit institutions, payment service providers, and insurers in 2024. In the case of serious deficiencies, it imposed capital surcharges.

As of January 17, 2025, the provisions of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) apply. The new EU Directive DORA imposes stricter requirements on the cyber resilience of financial institutions. In 2024, BaFin carried out extensive implementation work in this regard.

To create a fast, direct, and confidential exchange of information with companies in the financial sector during cyber crises, BaFin organized the first Cyber Crisis Roundtable in July 2024. Representatives from BaFin and eleven major companies from the German banking, insurance, and securities industries participated in the meeting. The exchange format is to be further expanded to include medium-sized companies and to promote dialogue beyond crisis situations.

Furthermore, BaFin was also active in the National Cyber Defense Center and exchanged information closely with other national and international authorities. It conducted a two-day cyber crisis exercise, testing together with selected companies from the financial industry and the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Federal Ministry of Finance, and the BSI how Germany's financial system could respond in a coordinated manner to a serious cyberattack.

1.5 Risks from Inadequate Money Laundering Prevention

The risks of financial sector companies being misused for money laundering purposes remain high. Particularly in international payment transactions, there is a high risk of money laundering and terrorist financing. Complex product and transaction structures also increase the risks.

BaFin further intensified its preventive supervision. It conducted routine and event-driven special audits in the banking and non-banking sectors. In 2024, BaFin focused more on high-risk products and business models.

The risks of being misused for terrorist financing have increased significantly in recent years due to the unstable geopolitical situation. Therefore, in its supervisory activities in 2024, BaFin placed particular emphasis on combating terrorist financing and underscored this at its anti-money laundering conference.

1 Personal Details
On January 1, 2024, insurance specialist Julia Wiens took over as Executive Director in charge of the Insurance and Pension Fund Supervision at BaFin. Her predecessor, Dr. Frank Grund, retired at the end of 2023. On December 11, 2024, BaFin also announced that the contract of Mark Branson as President of BaFin had been extended prematurely until 2029, and that risk management expert Nikolas Speer would take over the management of the Banking Supervision division on April 1, 2025. Raimund Röseler, the current Executive Director of BaFin's Banking Supervision, will retire at the end of March 2025.
2 Personnel
As of December 31, 2024, a total of 2,996 employees worked at BaFin (see Table 30, page 64). BaFin hired 191 new employees, most of whom came from the faculties of Economics, Law and Administration, Natural Sciences, and Computer Science. By the end of the year, 39 employees were engaged in long-term positions at international institutions and supervisory authorities. Ten of them were working as temporary assignees at the European Central Bank (ECB).

translation.en_XX:
I
At a Glance
BaFin Risks Focus 2024
In its annual report, BaFin explains what it undertakes to best mitigate these risks
"Risks in Focus at BaFin," which risks could most endanger the integrity and stability of the German financial system. BaFin dedicates special attention to these risks – in the sense of risk-oriented supervision. Future risks or trends are also described in the Risks in Focus. Moreover, BaFin explains therein that it provides a regular data-based market overview and analyzed individual funds based on monthly capital flow reports from investment management companies under stressed assumptions. In 2024, there was generally enough liquidity in real estate funds.

The insurance supervision conducted a comprehensive survey on the investment behavior of insurance companies in April and May 2024. Due to adverse market developments in the commercial real estate sector, a particular focus was on collecting quantitative data on this segment.

BaFin's analysis showed that the surveyed insurers had made negative valuation adjustments (fair values) of approximately 7 percent on average for commercial real estate, particularly office properties, as of December 31, 2023, compared to the year-end value of 2022.

A differentiated picture emerged in the financing of real estate projects: Here, the need for value adjustments among the surveyed insurers was on average about 11.5 percent. Consequently, insurers in this area had to make increased extraordinary write-downs. However, the total volume of such investments was comparatively low, so the required value corrections appeared to be manageable for the affected companies overall.

On the residential real estate market, the increased interest rates and high inflation since 2022 had an impact on prices. A portion of the overvaluations that had arisen in previous years was thus reduced. Over the course of 2024, there were clear signs of a decline in risks in the residential real estate market.

1.2 Risks from significant corrections in the international financial markets

The international financial markets proved to be stable in 2024 despite individual turbulences. Central banks' monetary policies were relaxed due to falling inflation. Interest rate cuts in Europe and the USA were expected by market participants and had already been priced in.

In early August 2024, there were short-term market collapses due to the unwinding of carry trades after the Japanese central bank slightly raised interest rates. The losses from these market movements were largely recovered within a short period. Nevertheless, the incident showed that the market can be very volatile.

The high public debt in many countries also posed risks to the financial system. Increased interest rates raised financing costs and default risk. This was reflected in the markets by the rising risk premiums on government bonds of these countries.

BaFin identified institutions with high and risky financial market-dependent exposures. It assessed the engagements in terms of their risk content and closely monitored the invested institutions – if necessary.

1.3 Risks from the default of corporate loans

The German economy continued to navigate difficult waters in 2024. After a decline in economic performance in recent years, very low growth is forecasted for 2025.

"2 Insurers and Pension Funds
II
2.1 New Foundations of Supervisory Practice
Sixth Regulation Amending Regulations under the Insurance Supervision Act
On July 24, 2024, the Sixth Regulation Amending Regulations under the Insurance Supervision Act was published in the Federal Law Gazette. It included a change to the Provision for Coverage Regulation (DeckRV), which sets the maximum permissible discount rate (Höchstrechnungszins – HRZ) for the calculation of the provision for coverage. For the first time in 30 years, the HRZ was increased on January 1, 2025: from 0.25 percent to 1.0 percent. The HRZ for guarantees in new business was also raised accordingly for pension funds in the Pension Fund Supervisory Regulation (PFAV).

Furthermore, the absolute lower limits for the minimum capital requirement for insurers within the scope of Solvency II were adjusted in the Capital Equipment Regulation (KapAusstV). With this, the Federal Ministry of Finance followed a corresponding announcement by the European Commission.

Seventh Regulation Amending Regulations under the Insurance Supervision Act
The Seventh Regulation Amending Regulations under the Insurance Supervision Act came into force on December 17, 2024. With changes to the Insurance Reporting Regulation (BerVersV), the KapAusstV, and the PFAV, BaFin has adapted the technical requirements of the reporting system in particular. The main regulatory content is the conversion of the reporting system to the XBRL format (eXtensible Business Reporting Language).

Circular on the Electronic Transmission of Asset Register Entries
On September 18, 2024, BaFin published Circular 02/2024 (VA) on the electronic transmission of entries made in the asset register. It assists primary insurance companies and pension funds in the uniform electronic transmission of their asset register entries to the supervisory authority. The companies must apply the contents of the circular for the first time for the electronic transmission of the asset register for the fiscal year 2024, which takes place in 2025.

2.2 Development in Individual Sectors
Behavior-Based Supervision
Following the publication of the information sheet 01/2023 on behavior-based supervisory aspects of capital-forming life insurance products, BaFin has so far conducted an in-depth review of 13 life insurers. In doing so, it pursued its risk-oriented supervisory approach. Thus, BaFin has already taken a closer look at a good 20 percent of the providers of capital-forming life insurance (excluding pension funds).

BaFin expects the products to offer an appropriate customer benefit for the target market, i.e., meet the security needs and/or return expectations of the customers. Especially for unit-linked products, companies must formulate return targets that can be achieved with sufficient probability. If it is to be expected that a significant portion of customers will terminate the contract prematurely, companies must take this into account when examining customer benefits.

At the end of August 2024, BaFin informed the public about the results of its previous investigations in this area and published a list with FAQs on its website.

Results of the Survey on Elemental Damage Coverage in Residential Building Insurance
Twelve selected residential building insurers had to answer a catalog of questions from BaFin regarding elemental damage coverage in residential building insurance. In the insurers' statements, BaFin found no supervisory deficiencies.
In 2024, all twelve insurers offered the inclusion of the elemental damage clause in private residential buildings in flood hazard classes 1 to 3 of the zoning system ZÜRS Geo 2023 through the opt-out model. This means that customers must consciously decline protection against elemental damage if they do not wish to have it. Thus, the insurance industry is fulfilling its promise to offer insurance protection in new business to almost all private homeowners as a fully integrated residential building insurance. The goal is to significantly increase the currently low coverage rate for elemental damages.

Cooperation within the Banking Union and in the European Union. Phase 2 focused on additional EU-specific reporting requirements and political mandates.

In the European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS), BaFin contributes its expertise to numerous working groups of European and global bodies. The EBA also continued to prepare for the application of MiCAR and DORA in 2024. In both cases, the EBA assumes direct supervisory functions for the first time and specifies the law through texts at Level 2 and 3.

European Cooperation in the Banking Union
BaFin is part of the Banking Union within the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) and the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM). Together with the other European Supervisory Authorities and the European Central Bank, the EBA participated in the cross-sectoral EU climate scenario analysis "Fit-For-55". The results were published on the EBA's website. The EBA also worked on guidelines for the management of ESG risks, which were consulted at the beginning of the year.

BaFin President Mark Branson sits on the Supervisory Board of the SSM. Birgit Rodolphe, Executive Director for Resolution and Anti-Money Laundering, is a member of the plenary session of the Single Resolution Board (SRB).

The European System of Financial Supervision
The European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS) includes the three European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs) and the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB), in which BaFin is represented at the leadership and working levels.

Technical Cooperation
In 2024, BaFin supervised various bilateral projects. Noteworthy is the administrative partnership with the Ukrainian securities regulator NSSMC. BaFin and the NSSMC conducted four workshops, and BaFin invited its Ukrainian colleagues for a study visit. For the Ukrainian central bank (National Bank of Ukraine – NBU), BaFin organized workshops on topics such as Non-Bank Financial Intermediation (NBFI) and insurance supervision.

2.7.2 The Work of the European Supervisory Authorities and the European Systemic Risk Board
The EBA
The European Banking Authority (EBA) focused on implementing mandates from the banking package. This includes the revised Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) and the revised EU Capital Requirements Directive (CRD). The EBA divided the high number of work assignments related to this package into two phases. In the first phase, the EBA addressed the mandates for the final implementation of Basel III.

The EIOPA
The European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) conducted its regular stress test in 2024 and published the results. They show that the European insurance sector is well-capitalized overall and has sufficient liquid assets. The results also demonstrate that the included German companies have sufficient liquid assets to cover their liquidity needs in the stress scenario.

EIOPA also published a report on the prudential treatment of sustainability risks for insurers and proposed higher capital backing for shares and bonds in fossil fuels. In addition, EIOPA published an Opinion on the (re)assessment of the NatCat standard formula. To close insurance coverage gaps in natural disasters, EIOPA intends to become more visible as a Data Hub in the future.

With EIOPA's benchmark methodology published in 2024, the appropriate customer benefit is addressed, an important focus in BaFin's conduct supervision.

BaFin Executive Director Julia Wiens (Insurance Supervision) is a member of the Board of Supervisors of EIOPA and was elected to the EIOPA Management Board in November 2024.

Insider Trading
BaFin works closely with public prosecutors and police authorities to prosecute individuals who commit insider trading offenses. Tables 12 and 13 show how insider investigations and completed insider proceedings developed in 2024.

Since the tightening of criminal asset recovery that came into effect on July 1, 2017, legal remedies have been exhausted in a large part of the proceedings for insider trading offenses. Therefore, it often takes a long time for legally binding decisions to be made. These proceedings are not yet listed in BaFin's statistics.

Courts now punish insider trading much more severely than in the first decades after the introduction of the legal prohibition in 1994. For example, in the past year, several custodial sentences were pronounced that were not suspended for probation. In addition, there were several suspended custodial sentences. Following the Federal Court of Justice's fundamental decision on December 6, 2023, regarding the confiscation of assets in insider trading, it is expected that the remaining pending proceedings can be concluded in the foreseeable future.

In 2024, BaFin published four announcements on ordered special audits. In addition, it made ten findings of errors public. In the previous year, there were three announcements and 14 findings of errors.

Publication of Financial Reports

The BaFin also prepared for the supervision of instruments that fall under the new EU Regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCAR). Since June 2024, it has been supervising issuers of certain tokens and since December 2024 also crypto-asset service providers. 

1.8 Trend: Sustainability
Climate and environmental risks remained a challenge for the financial sector in 2024. In particular, physical climate risks resulting from the specific effects of climate change, such as extreme weather events, cause enormous financial and personal damage and can affect, for example, the credit portfolios of banks or the damage sums of insurers. Risks of greenwashing also continued to pose a significant risk to investors' trust in a functioning financial market.

These risks must be adequately considered to ensure the stability of the financial system. Companies must adapt their business models to the changing conditions and strengthen their resilience to climate and environmental risks.

In 2024, BaFin took various measures to promote the consideration of climate and environmental risks in the financial sector. These include, among other things, intensified supervisory work on the handling of potentially particularly exposed banks and insurers with physical risks and the further development of supervisory stress tests. For example, questions on ESG were included in the supplementary qualitative questionnaire of the LSI stress test. A particular focus in 2024 was also on improving data quality and developing suitable methods for assessing climate and environmental risks within the framework of risk management.

Focus on Disclosure and Reporting
Another focus was on reviewing the implementation of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR). One of the most common findings: The disclosed information on the sustainability impact of products and services was not always understandable enough.

Furthermore, BaFin expanded its competencies to meet the new requirements of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). This directive leads to more comprehensive and comparable sustainability reporting by companies once it is transposed into national law.

BaFin actively participated in the European discussion on the further development of the EU Disclosure Regulation SFDR and brought its expertise to relevant bodies. The goal is to create simplified, understandable, and uniform standards for sustainable financial products and services and to prevent greenwashing.

1.9 Trend: Geopolitical Upheavals
Geopolitical tensions pose a growing threat to the global economy. Rising energy prices, supply chain problems, and cyber-attacks are just some of the consequences. In addition, a global security and economic order based on free trade and rules is increasingly being questioned. This strengthens geopolitical uncertainties and tensions. Germany, with its strong export orientation and international networking, is particularly vulnerable to geopolitical shocks.

The financial industry is directly and indirectly affected: Cyber-attacks can directly hit companies. Indirect consequences for the financial sector companies arise when the economic environment deteriorates and volatility in the financial markets increases.

In 2024, BaFin examined the risks that could arise for German companies and banks from geopolitical events. It focused particularly on loans granted to companies in certain regions or industries that are especially vulnerable to political uncertainties.

The most frequent complaint topic, as in the previous year, was the nature of claims processing by credit institutions and financial service providers, including delayed processing or delayed payout of insurance benefits. In 2024, a significant proportion of complaints were also related to the "Motor Vehicle" insurance sector. There was also a noticeable increase in complaints in private health insurance.

Although the number of complaints and inquiries regarding credit and financial service institutions decreased compared to the previous year, it remained high in 2024: A total of 22,366 complaints and inquiries were received by BaFin (see Graphic 1), of which 22,123 were complaints (see Table 19) and 243 were inquiries. Many complaints concerned the branches of a credit institution. This issue had already occupied BaFin in 2023. In addition, there were many complaints about the limited customer service of online institutions.

Securities Business

translation.en_XX:
At a Glance V
Who is responsible?
1 Settlement in the Banking Union
In the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM), there are two responsibilities: the central task of BaFin as the national resolution authority and the IRTs is to improve the resolvability of institutions. To this end, resolution plans are drawn up and updated annually. Furthermore, it is assessed which obstacles may hinder a possible resolution and how these could be eliminated.

BaFin as the national resolution authority
BaFin is responsible for German institutions that are classified as not significant by the European Central Bank (ECB) (Less Significant Institutions – LSIs). In addition, as a resolution authority, it also takes responsibility for financial market infrastructures with banking licenses and for central counterparties with and without banking licenses.

Single Resolution Board (SRB)
In contrast to BaFin, the SRB in the SRM is only responsible for the resolution of credit institutions that fall under the European Capital Requirements Regulation. Its responsibilities include
■ institutions classified as significant by the ECB (Significant Institutions – SIs),
■ cross-border active LSIs, and
■ LSIs for which the responsibility has been transferred to the SRB.

For each institution or group of institutions under its jurisdiction, the SRB has established internal resolution teams (Internal Resolution Teams – IRTs). In these teams, the SRB and the respective national resolution authorities work together. In 2024, BaFin participated in 34 IRTs.

2 Settlement in the European Union and Cooperation with Third-Country Authorities
The SRB and/or the national resolution authorities establish resolution colleges to coordinate the cooperation of various resolution authorities in the Banking Union, in the EU, and in third countries. These forums generally take place whenever affected groups operate beyond the borders of the Banking Union in at least one other member state of the European Union. In 2024, BaFin participated in 21 resolution colleges.

For all institutions classified by the Financial Stability Board (FSB) as globally systemically important (Global Systemically Important Banks – G-SIBs), Crisis Management Groups (CMGs) are established. In 2024, 29 institutions were classified as G-SIBs worldwide, with 21 of them active in Germany. BaFin participated in a total of 16 CMGs in 2024.

2 Resolution Planning
BaFin is represented in internal resolution teams of the Single Resolution Board (SRB) within the SRM. In the 2024 resolution planning cycle, BaFin staff were involved in 34 internal resolution teams (Internal Resolution Teams – IRTs). 18 IRTs were responsible for institutions based in Germany and 16 for institution groups based abroad (see info box "Who is responsible?").

The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) addressed, among other things, current developments in the field of artificial intelligence and crypto assets in 2024. It also focused on supervisory approaches to transition plans and financial products promoted as sustainable.

Liability Branches. These insurance branches account for a significant portion of the total premium volume in property and casualty insurance. In 2024, the average premiums in these branches increased significantly in some cases. However, in motor vehicle insurance, insurers passed on the necessary premium increases to policyholders only with a delay.

According to preliminary figures, profitability in the overall market improved slightly in 2024 compared to the previous year. The combined net loss/cost ratio, which essentially indicates the ratio of claims expenses to premium income, is slightly below the 100 percent mark.

In terms of solvency, property and casualty insurers were able to cope well with the relatively high claims inflation overall. The SCR coverage changed little in 2024.

2.2.4 Development of Reinsurance Companies

Reinsurers increased premiums again in 2024, both in the motor vehicle sector and for the insurance of natural catastrophes. In the motor vehicle sector, the costs of spare parts and repairs rose noticeably. Elemental damage increased due to more frequent natural catastrophes and the continued high construction costs. In 2024, BaFin also discussed with the supervised companies the price stability in the reinsurance of natural catastrophes, combined with the increase in deductibles for primary insurers.

Due to the high demand for reinsurance protection, alternative forms of risk transfer, such as catastrophe bonds (Cat-Bonds) and insurance-linked securities (ILS), gained importance in 2024 as well. The SCR coverage of German reinsurers declined slightly over the course of 2024, falling from 284.3 percent in 2023 to 282.6 percent in 2024. At the same time, the gross loss-cost ratio of the largest German reinsurers decreased moderately from 95.6 percent to 93.4 percent.

2.2.5 Development of Pension Funds and Pension Schemes

Pension schemes, particularly affected by the long-term low-interest environment, were relieved by the interim rise in interest rates. Their earnings opportunities in new investments and reinvestments improved. However, their hidden reserves decreased, and many schemes incurred hidden burdens.

BaFin's forecast calculation as of September 30, 2024, showed an overall further improved development for the industry. Depending on the scenario, the situation remains tense for some pension schemes. The number of schemes under intensified supervision decreased slightly and remained below 20 at the end of the year. According to the forecast, two pension schemes were unable to meet the solvency requirements as of December 31, 2024.

Pension Funds

Pension funds were overall less affected by the low-interest phase than pension schemes. Economically, all pension funds were able to cope with the four scenarios of the forecast calculation as of September 30, 2024. In the insurance-like business, where pension funds themselves bear the risk for fulfilling the obligations, the rise in interest rates led to hidden burdens. All 35 pension funds supervised by BaFin had sufficient own funds for the fiscal year 2024 and for the following four fiscal years according to the forecast calculation. For about two-thirds of the supervised pension funds, the regulatory required own funds were equivalent to the minimum amount of the Minimum Capital Requirement: For stock corporations, this amounts to three million euros, for mutual pension fund associations to 2.25 million euros.

I
The European Securities and Markets Authority member on the Administrative Board of the ESRB.
(European Securities and Markets Authority – ESMA)
set a clear sign for progress in the 2.7.3 Work of the global standard setters
further development of the internal market: The ESMA directed
20 specific proposals to the EU Commission and the legislators in Brussels. BaFin is also a member of the global standard
setters. In their top committees, the respective competent Executive Directors of BaFin
are represented. BaFin President Mark Branson represents BaFin in the Plenary of the Financial Stability Board.

On the topic of sustainability, ESMA delivered three
important products in 2024: the guidelines on fund names, the final report on greenwashing, and a vision for
a sustainable future. With regard to market infrastructure, ESMA recommends shortening the standard settlement cycle for the EU, in line with
major financial markets abroad. This would accelerate the settlement of transactions from two days (T+2) to one day (T+1).

ESMA attested to BaFin's successful implementation of the lessons learned from the Wirecard AG case in the follow-up to the Peer Review from 2020. In the final report, ESMA praised the efforts of the German
legislators and BaFin. In particular, it highlighted that BaFin has received the necessary intervention powers and has set up its new organizational structure for better information exchange.

BaFin Executive Director Dr. Thorsten Pötzsch (Securities Supervision/Asset Management) is a member of the Board of Supervisors of ESMA, as well as a member of the Management Board and Chairman of the ESMA Sustainability Standing Committee.

The ESRB
The European Systemic Risk Board (European Systemic Risk Board – ESRB) published a report in 2024 as part of its strategy to strengthen the European financial sector against cyber risks, analyzing appropriate tools. It focused on measures for information exchange and coordination at the national and European level. In addition, the ESRB addressed possible safeguard systems for critical functions in the event of widespread cyber incidents.

The ESRB also continued its work on measuring systemic liquidity risks and published a final report at the beginning of 2025.

BaFin participates in the ESRB working groups in the analysis of current issues such as stress test scenarios and the financial intermediation of non-bank financial institutions (NBFI).

The BCBS
The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision – BCBS) celebrated its 50th anniversary at the 23rd International Conference of Banking Supervisors on April 24 and 25, 2024. There, representatives of supervisory authorities and central banks from over 90 jurisdictions adopted the revised Basel Core Principles, which represent the global standard for sound banking regulation and supervision. These principles define the minimum standard for financial systems and are used, among other things, by the International Monetary Fund to assess the effectiveness of the banking sector.

The members of the BCBS continued to work through the banking sector turbulence of 2023 in 2024. It monitored potential risks to financial stability and analyzed, among other things, liquidity and interest rate change risks. It also exchanged experiences with supervisors from member countries.

In 2024, the BCBS also continued to monitor the implementation of the final Basel III reforms. Despite delays, the EU agreed in 2024 on the corresponding revision of the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR), so that the Basel reforms could be applied for the first time in Europe on January 1, 2025. Transition periods until the end of 2032 are intended to assist banks with the implementation.

In various consultation papers, the BCBS discussed proposals for solving the window dressing problem in the determination of globally systemically important banks. This refers to the phenomenon that banks can shape their balance sheet through legally permitted transactions before the balance sheet date as follows: They create the appearance that their global systemic importance is lower and therefore lower systemic risk buffers would be justified. With the reform, the BCBS is trying to prevent this possibility.

Executive Director Raimund Röseler represented BaFin in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.

For the first time, MaRisk for payment and e-money institutions includes the German banking market, which comprises large as well as many small credit institutions. The BaFin published on May 27, 2024, for the first time, minimum requirements for the risk management of institutions that fall under the Payment Services Supervision Act (ZAG-MaRisk). With ZAG-MaRisk, BaFin makes it clear that payment and e-money institutions need appropriate risk management. In addition, it provides institutions with a flexible and practical framework for the design of proper business organization.

The transition period for the implementation of this circular ended on January 1, 2025. An important interim result of this process: the supervisory communication of November 26, 2024. In it, the supervisory authority introduced new facilitations for small institutions, such as in stress tests or reporting. It also points out existing leeways that banks do not always use and has significantly expanded the circle of users. BaFin shows with concrete examples that small institutions can design their risk management processes less elaborately without impairing the effective control of their risks.

ZAG: BaFin publishes circular on reporting risks in payment transactions
On April 26, 2024, BaFin published a circular for payment service providers. It specifies how they must report operational and security-related risks according to § 53 paragraph 2 of the Payment Services Supervision Act (ZAG).

FAQ on the Remuneration Ordinance for Institutions published
On June 13, 2024, BaFin published questions and answers (FAQ) on the Remuneration Ordinance for Institutions. It takes into account guidelines of the EBA on remuneration. The questions and answers replace the previous interpretation aid for the Remuneration Ordinance for Institutions. Institutions must, among other things, apply the guidelines for a sound remuneration policy according to Directive 2013/36/EU directly. The FAQ also contains matters not covered by the EBA guidelines or concerning their proportional implementation.

Cooperative banks: BaFin publishes general ruling on instruments of hard core capital
A new general ruling by BaFin regulates the extent to which newly issued business shares in cooperative banks can be classified as instruments of hard core capital with BaFin's permission. In the version valid since January 1, 2024, BaFin also stipulates under what conditions the repayment of business assets due to terminated cooperative shares is pre-approved.

Supervisory communication on proportionality
BaFin advocates for regulation and supervision that is as unbureaucratic and proportional as possible.10 The German cooperative banking sector includes large, but also many small credit institutions. For these, the existing regulation is too complex, complicated, and extensive. Some small institutions have to meet requirements that are not relevant to them. This can lead to overload, is not cost-adequate, and contradicts the principle of reconciling risk control with business aspects. Against this background – and after intensive discussions with the industry – BaFin has critically reviewed and adjusted its administrative practice.

Supervisory communication SREP 2024: New surcharge classes for determining the capital requirements
Since 2016, BaFin, together with the Deutsche Bundesbank, has been setting the SREP overall capital requirement (Pillar 2 Requirement, P2R) for institutions under national supervision. For this purpose, it also determined surcharge classes for the other significant risks in 2024. The basis for this activity is the European Capital Requirements Directive IV (CRD IV). This introduced the Pillar II overall capital requirement, which is implemented in §§ 6c and 6d of the Banking Act (KWG). SREP stands for Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process.

Supervisory communication on the Secondary Credit Market Act: Licensing procedure for credit service institutions
An important goal of the Secondary Credit Market Act (KrZwMG) is to protect borrowers. Therefore, in its supervisory communication of March 26, 2024, BaFin pointed out the importance of consumer protection-related organizational obligations that credit service institutions must fulfill.

translation.en_XX:
The BaFin has updated the general part of the interpretative notes and early warning system and transparency through the storage database and published it on November 29, 2024. Transparency about the interconnections in the financial market is therefore important for BaFin to be able to estimate the potential extent of an incident.

In April 2024, the European legislator adopted the three central parts of an anti-money laundering package. This laid the foundation for the harmonization of supervisory requirements for the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing. BaFin is intensively preparing for the new European supervisory regime and is actively involved in the preparations for the implementation of the new European anti-money laundering regime.3

1.6 Risks from concentrations in the outsourcing of IT services

In 2024, outsourcing by financial sector companies continued to increase – especially outsourcing to IT multi-tenant service providers. While companies can reduce costs and focus on their core business through outsourcing, on the other hand, strong dependence on a few specialized IT service providers can pose significant risks.

The concentration on a few providers means that, for example, disruptions at just one service provider or its failure can have consequences for a large number of financial sector companies, as many companies depend on its services. This is particularly true for critical processes on which the functioning of the financial market depends. This can lead to greater vulnerability of the entire financial market.

The focus of BaFin and other financial supervisory authorities is on IT multi-tenant service providers, on which the companies of the financial market depend. If such multi-tenant service providers fail, switching to another service provider is often difficult and time-consuming, as specialized solutions cannot be easily replaced. Reintegration into the company itself is also not possible in many cases due to specialization.

1.7 Trend: Advancing digitalization

As described, new technologies offer opportunities for the financial industry but also carry risks such as bias in AI models, dependence on large technology providers, and potential dangers to financial stability.

Companies in the financial industry are increasingly using Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, across the entire value chain. Many initiatives for the use of generative AI are still in the testing or pilot phase. In 2024, BaFin intensively examined the use of AI in the financial sector to better assess risks. The focus was particularly on generative AI.

However, the financial services sector is already exploring various potential practical applications, for example in risk management and portfolio optimization. A potential breakthrough in quantum computing poses risks for the financial sector. Companies must prepare for this development now, as quantum computers can decrypt classical encryption methods.

BaFin also examined the impact of Open Finance on the German financial market and the importance of open financial data for the industry and supervision.

1.2 Prospectuses
Accelerated Share Prospectus Procedures
BaFin monitors information obligations from the EU Green Bond Regulation
Since December 2024, European Green Bonds can be issued under the special transparency requirements of the Regulation (EU) 2023/2631 (EUGBR). In addition, the EUGBR also contains optional transparency regulations for other types of ecologically sustainable bonds. BaFin supervises whether issuers fulfill their EUGBR information obligations. However, BaFin does not verify the substantive accuracy of the information, such as the taxonomy conformity of the planned use of proceeds.

Since August 2024, BaFin has been offering issuers the opportunity to significantly accelerate their share prospectus procedures. The duration of the procedure from the initial submission to the approval of the prospectus can thus be reduced to six to eight weeks. This requires that the issuer and BaFin coordinate in detail in advance and that the issuer provides an almost complete version of the prospectus at the time of initial submission.

Since then, the accelerated procedure has mostly been applied, particularly by issuers in the regulated market. With this offer, BaFin is making the process more efficient.

1 Highlights of the Supervisory Strategy

1.1 Risks from corrections in the values of collateral burdened their balance sheets. The situation in the US commercial real estate market, where some German banks have invested, exacerbated this situation. The BaFin will continue to closely supervise institutions that have focused their business on the commercial real estate market.

The situation in the German commercial real estate market, including commercial residential properties, remained tense in 2024. The market for commercial real estate is highly correlated with the weaker economic environment. Insolvencies of commercial tenants, property holders, and project developers are increasingly leading to loan defaults. This was reflected in the rising rates of non-performing loans (NPLs) at German credit institutions, both at significant institutions (SIs) and less significant institutions (LSIs). Banks with a focus on the financing of commercial real estate were particularly at risk, as loan defaults and declining collateral values increased.

In contrast, the residential real estate market showed signs of stabilization. Prices rose slightly, and new lending began to recover slowly. Loss rates remained low, and risk provisioning only increased moderately.

The market environment for real estate funds remained challenging due to further capital outflows from open public funds. Therefore, in April 2024, BaFin established new regulations.

translation.en_XX:
The general order was still subject to judicial clarification at the editorial deadline. The Administrative Court of Frankfurt granted the complaint of six model plaintiffs in October 2024 and lifted the general order for them. The court did not see any consumer protection relevant misconduct within the meaning of BaFin's authorization basis. BaFin has appealed against this judgment.

Another market investigation conducted by BaFin in 2024 focused on turbo certificates. Turbo certificates are leveraged products traded on the stock exchange. The investigation revealed, among other things, that three out of four customers lost money trading turbo certificates. In total, the losses from 2019 to 2023 amounted to around 3.4 billion euros. Based on the information obtained, a review process for possible product intervention measures was initiated. It is being examined whether turbo certificates pose significant investor protection concerns for private customers.

Violated WpHG obligations: BaFin imposes fines
In May 2024, BaFin imposed a fine of 12,975,000 euros on an institution that had violated the obligations of the Securities Trading Act (WpHG) (§ 80 paragraph 2 sentence 3 number 1 and number 2 WpHG). The institution did not have suitable systems and risk controls to ensure that its trading systems were subject to appropriate trading thresholds and limits. As a result, a manual input error in the order system was not detected, which led to the transmission of erroneous orders. A market disruption was the consequence.

Furthermore, in July 2024, BaFin imposed a fine of 830,000 euros on the German branch of an institution that had violated, among other things, the obligations of the WpHG (§ 63 paragraph 7 to 9, § 64 paragraph 3). It had not informed all customers about the costs and incidental costs of specific financial instruments during the fiscal year 2019/2020 when providing securities services. In addition, the institution provided securities services without sufficiently checking relevant information from customers about their financial circumstances during the suitability assessment.

2.4.4 Market monitoring
Market investigation certificates
In 2024, BaFin investigated the sales of interest and express certificates, which were sold more to consumers after the interest rate turnaround. For this purpose, it conducted market investigations with manufacturers and distribution companies and surveyed consumers. In one of the market investigations, it was examined to what extent they complied with legal requirements for the design of investment certificates and how they distributed these products. For the first time, BaFin also surveyed customers of banks and savings banks who had purchased such products.

The investigations by BaFin found no evidence that banks and savings banks had pressured customers interested in deposit products into certificates.

Online survey on the relevance of social media for financial topics
In May 2024, BaFin asked a total of 1,000 consumers between the ages of 18 and 45 how they inform themselves about financial topics.

It turned out that users of social media invest significantly more often in risky products such as crypto assets. Another finding: influencers and finfluencers not only convey information. They also manage to animate young people to buy the products they promote.

Mystery shopping for insurance investment products
In a mystery shopping action coordinated by EIOPA, BaFin tested the distribution of insurance investment products in 2024. The focus was on life and pension insurances whose value depends on market fluctuations. The action focused on advisory and information obligations. The results were not yet available at the editorial deadline.

Survey on over-indebtedness in real estate financing
In the fall of 2024, BaFin surveyed more than 3,000 consumers on the topic of real estate financing.

Among other things, it emerged that about four out of five respondents who were looking for real estate financing sought professional advice. About 90 percent were satisfied with the advice and felt well informed about the risks of financing. More than half of those who were currently financing a property found it difficult to meet their living costs and monthly installments. Around 15 percent of respondents who were financing a property on their own spent more than 40 percent of their monthly net income to pay the installments.
